claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by enhanced dislocation nucleation at FCC/BCC heterointerfaces.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by dislocation accumulation at FCC/BCC heterointerfaces.
Severe lattice distortion locally lowers the energy barrier for dislocation emission.
Short-range order locally lowers the energy barrier for dislocation emission.
Lower barriers for dislocation emission enable sequential activation of slip systems.
Dislocations form interfacial networks that drive creep.
The starting coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The starting multilayer possesses severe lattice distortion.
The starting multilayer possesses short-range compositional order.
A sustained sub-yield load at 400–600°C can enable creep while preserving the nanoscale multilayer structure.
Local compositional variations enhance dislocation generation and accumulation at FCC/BCC interfaces.
After nucleation, dislocations propagate within the constituent layers.
Propagating dislocations interact at interfaces and progressively form dislocation networks.
Interfacial dislocation networks mediate the creep process.
Deformation will significantly increase dislocation density relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Deformation will produce characteristic dislocation accumulations at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Creep strain-versus-time curves will show gradually accelerating deformation correlated with the evolution of interfacial dislocation networks.
The as-deposited baseline has relatively uniform dislocation density and no pronounced interfacial dislocation networks.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture is retained and recrystallization, grain growth, and catastrophic failure are avoided.
